title: The judge
hookLine: a judge rules in disputes, bound by evidence

lines: I AM ONLY A HUMAN BEING.
ONE ARGUES BETTER THAN THE OTHER.
cards: I am only a human being. That's not a defendant talking. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, it's the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, speaking as a judge.
People bring their quarrels to him, he says, and one of them may argue his case better than the other, so he rules by what he hears.

Then a warning to whoever wins: if I hand you something that's really your brother's, I'm handing you a piece of fire. A judge who admits he can be fooled, and puts the weight back on the people in front of him.

teach.b: A qadi is a judge, the one who decides between people. Yesterday's mufti gives an answer, and the asker can weigh it. A qadi gives a ruling, and the parties in the case are bound by it.
The tradition fenced that heavier job with rules. First, the command.

teach.h: I JUDGE BY WHAT I HEAR.
teach.b: Surah four, in Pickthall's translation: "if ye judge between mankind, that ye judge justly." Second, the hadith from the hook. The Prophet judges by what he hears.
A ruling decides the case in front of the court; it doesn't turn a lie into the truth. The one who wins by clever talk still answers for what he took. Third, who has to prove what.
A saying gathered by an-Nawawi in his Forty Hadith, from al-Bayhaqi: if people were given whatever they claimed, some would claim the property and even the lives of others.

teach.h: PROOF ON THE ONE WHO CLAIMS.
teach.b: So the proof is on the one who makes the claim, and the oath is on the one who denies it. The judge starts from evidence, not a hunch, and when there's none, from an oath. Fourth, the judge's own state.
In Bukhari, a companion passes on the Prophet's words that a judge should not decide between two people while he is angry.
Not won over by the better speaker. Bound by what can be shown. Some scholars of the early generations are remembered for refusing the job of qadi altogether, because they feared its weight.
The tradition treats the seat as a trust, and an uncomfortable one.

how: In Islamic law a qadi, a judge, hears disputes and rules on the evidence; in some countries qadis or family courts still hear cases about marriage and inheritance, and Muslims elsewhere sometimes bring such matters to religious arbitration.

o: a scholar whose advice the one who asked may weigh
a judge whose ruling binds, decided by evidence and oath
a leader who stands in front to lead the prayer

p: a wrong share won by clever talk

s: the Prophet said a clever speaker could never mislead his rulings
he said: I am only a human being, and I judge by what I hear.
in the saying, the proof is on the one who makes the claim
and the oath is on the one who denies it.
a hadith in Bukhari says a judge should not decide while angry
not between two people while he is angry.

games.q: two people bring you a dispute. one argues brilliantly; the other stumbles over his words. what does the Prophet say about ruling between them?
o: the better speaker is usually the honest one.
I judge by what I hear, and a wrong share is a piece of fire.
leave every dispute to God and never rule.
games.why: in Bukhari he says he is only human and rules by what he hears; whoever wins what's really his brother's is taking a piece of fire.

practice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're part of right now and sit in the judge's seat: what do you actually know, what are you assuming, and what would the other person say if they spoke as well as you do?
If you're angry, just notice it, and let one breath out longer than the rest; if you pray, you can ask in your own words to be fair.

wordCard.voice: Qadi. A judge who rules in disputes, bound by evidence: proof from the one who claims, an oath from the one who denies. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a judge, the one who decides between people in a dispute.

carryVoice: Your line: judge by evidence. What can be shown, not what sounds best. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: if ye judge between mankind, that ye judge justly
